 by BARBARA MORSE, NBC10

 (WJAR) — The debate over changing our clocks twice a year continues, with supporters of permanent daylight saving time pointing to brighter evenings and medical experts emphasizing the benefits of morning light.
 The Sunshine Protection Act, a proposal in Congress, would make daylight saving time permanent, keeping it lighter later in the day.
 But many medical experts say that schedule does not align with our circadian rhythm.
 "It is our body's time keeping mechanism and it's set not by something on our wrist, but it's set by the sun rising and falling," explained Dr. Jared Saletin, associate director at the Bradley Hospital Sleep Research Laboratory.
 Like many others in his field, Saletin supports standard time, which is now in effect.
 "The benefit of that for us is we get our morning light back," Saletin said.
 "Those morning light hours are necessary not only for us to wake up and feel healthy and happy but there really is almost a safety issue for folks that are trying to go to work, trying to go to school, go to the school bus, those morning light hours are going to be very beneficial."
 That one-hour difference, he said, can have wide-ranging effects.
 "It doesn't just dictate when we go to bed and when we wake up, the circadian rhythm actually governs almost all the tissues in our body, how our gut metabolizes what we eat to how our physical activity and physical strength fluctuates throughout the day and yes to our mental acuity, to our mood, to our attention," Saletin said.
 Standard time, however, also brings earlier sunsets, increasing risks for pedestrians, cyclists and animals as drivers adjust to darker evening commutes.

 Dr. Daniel Shanin, medical director of the Anderson Emergency Center at Rhode Island Hospital, said drivers should be especially vigilant in the coming weeks as everyone adjusts.
 "At the same time, the extra hour of sleep may help protect against some of the fatigue-related risks we see with the spring time change, when drivers lose an hour of sleep," Shanin said.
